items.html:
Bangladeshi licence plates are either white, black or turquoise.

NOTE: The turquoise plate can only be found in Bangladesh.

The Bengali script features a continuous horizontal line at the top of each word. It has a similar look to Devanagari (Hindi and Nepali), however it can usually be recognised by the many letters featuring triangular shapes.

NOTE: Bengali is an official language in Bangladesh and parts of eastern India.

In Generation 3 coverage, these three cars can be seen in Bangladesh: the red mirror with bars, classic white and striped white car.

NOTE: The classic white car is the only car that is not unique to Bangladesh. Make sure to not mix up the striped white with the Cambodian car, since they look similar.
In Generation 4 coverage, two Street View cars can be seen in Bangladesh: a black car and a white car.

Bangladesh, as well as a variety of other countries, has received some poor quality coverage, also known as “Shitcam”. The Shitcam car colours are black and white.

NOTE: Sometimes the car colour can be fully obstructed by a big circular blur.

Rickshaws are frequently found all around Bangladesh, especially the green auto rickshaws.

NOTE: They are found in other Asian countries as well.

Signposts in Bangladesh often have black-and-white stripes.

NOTE: Within Asia, these posts are also found in Sri Lanka, Bhutan, India, Nepal and Malaysia. Make sure to check other clues before guessing.
Bodies of water and agricultural fields can be often seen beside the streets of Bangladesh.
Streets in Bangladesh are often lined by trees, which sometimes have white paint on the bottom of their trunks.

Bangladesh uses red-and-white concrete bollards throughout the whole country.

NOTE: They can also be found in a square form instead of a circular form.

Tin roofs are commonly found in Bangladesh.

NOTE: Due to the humid climate, many countries in South and Southeast Asia use tin roofs.
The Generation 4 coverage in Bangladesh will often have a smoky feel to it.

Bangladesh has several distinct roof styles that create an east/west divide in the country.

The west, particularly the divisions of Rajshahi, Khulna and Dhaka, is dominated by hip roofs made of sheet metal. The states of Rangpur and Chittagong tend to have mixed roofs.

In the east, you will commonly see sheet metal roofs with a triangular "window" just below the ridge of the roof. The state of Sylhet will exclusively have this style, which can also be seen in Chittagong, Mymensingh, eastern Rangpur and northern Dhaka.
Tiled roofs are uncommon in Bangladesh, but the ones you do see are of West Bengal origin, and are thus only found on the Indian border in the state of Khulna.

Rice is the main agricultural crop in Bangladesh and is planted twice a year. The different rice seasons can be told apart by the height and colour of the rice and are very useful for regionguessing.

Short green rice that is barely sticking out of the water is known as early growth rice. Early growth rice can be seen in the states of Khulna, Mymensingh and south of Padma River in Dhaka.

NOTE: Beware that this, and the following tips, are only accurate in Generation 4 coverage.
Slightly taller rice, in the middle of growing, which still remains green, can be seen in the states of Rangpur, Barishal and Chittagong.

Fully-grown rice is characterised by being noticeably taller, as well as having a yellow or orange colour and fluffier tips - the fluffiness signifies that the rice is ripe. Fully-grown rice is mostly seen in the state of Rajshahi, but it is also present in Rangpur and Chittagong.

Harvested rice can be identified by its beige or brown colour and shorter, cut down appearance. It can be seen alongside fully-grown, unharvested rice as well as freshly planted early growth rice in adjacent fields. This is most commonly seen in the states of Sylhet and southern Khulna.

Rice fields require some rest time, so it's natural to come across some off-season barren, empty fields without rice altogether. Off-season fields are mostly seen in the state of Dhaka, north of Padma River.
Vast rice fields with almost nothing else in view can be seen in the border area between the states of Dhaka, Mymensingh and Sylhet.
While most of Bangladesh is almost completely flat, in the eastern parts of Chittagong you may find fairly tall, forested and uncultivated hills.
A sizable east-west ridge can be seen on the Indian border from the northern parts of Sylhet and eastern Mymensingh. It is often obscured or diminished by heavy haze.

Corn tends to be planted in the west of Bangladesh - large and medium-sized fields can be found in Rajshahi, Rangpur, western Mymensingh and northern Khulna.

Smaller patches of corn can be found in the south of Barishal, usually adjacent to other crops.

Jute is a tall-growing green crop which gets dried and used in the making of rugs, bags and other goods. Because of when the coverage was taken, jute can almost exclusively be found on Street View in Rangpur. In its dried state it can be found hanging off fences and drying on the roads anywhere in the country.

Canola is a low-growing crop with yellow flowers that is used to make cooking oil. It is usually planted during the off-season for rice, making it extremely common north of Padma river in the state of Dhaka.
Tea production in Bangladesh is concentrated in the highlands of southern Sylhet and, rarely, Chittagong.

Standalone fruit trees in Bangladesh are most commonly seen in the states of Rajshahi and Rangpur. Fruit orchards with systematically planted trees, however, are concentrated near the Indian border in both states.
Sunflower fields are found in the south of Barishal state.
Fields of watermelons can also be found in the south of Barishal.
Eucalyptus trees are tall trees with lush crowns and ivory-coloured trunks. In Bangladesh they are more common in the north, with Rangpur, Rajshahi and Mymensingh being the most likely states.

Blossoming trees are tied to coverage and seasonal metas in Bangladesh, and are only found in the states where coverage was taken during spring time - Khulna, Mymensingh and southern Dhaka.

NOTE: Beware that this is only accurate in Generation 4 coverage.

Beach Sheoaks (Casuarina equisetifolia) are thin evergreen trees with thin, long, drooping branchlets. Like the name suggests, they are mostly observed in coastal regions - along the coast of the Teknaf Peninsula and around Noakhali city in Chittagong.

For legal reasons, Google has added small labels noting their copyright on all Street View coverage. These labels contain a year, typically the year when the coverage was released, which can be used to regionguess Bangladesh. Generation 4 coverage with 2022 written on the copyright labels can be found in Mymensingh, Dhaka and less commonly Chittagong.

NOTE: Beware that the copyright labels will rarely get updated to a later year, without any other changes to the coverage.

Similarly, Generation 4 coverage with 2023 written on the copyright labels can be found in Rangpur, Rajshahi, Khulna, Barishal, Sylhet and less commonly Chittagong.

NOTE: 2024 and 2025 now make up around half of all copyright dates. These can be found all over the country.
Shitcam coverage is only found in and around Dhaka.
Generation 3 coverage with the white Street View car can be found in Dhaka, Chattogram as well as on the highway connecting them.
Generation 3 coverage with the striped Street View car can be found mostly on yellow roads west of Dhaka.
In the city of Sylhet there will often be a guard at the side of the car visible, usually holding a hayfork. Note that this only applies to Generation 3 coverage.

In the city of Barishal there can also be a guard at the side of the car visible, not to be confused with the Sylhet guard.

NOTE: The same man can rarely be found elsewhere on trekker coverage.
This interesting trekker with a black cover can be found in the city of Khulna.
The trekker with red colour in the mirrors is unique to the island of Nijhum Dwip.
A scooter trekker, where mostly the left mirror and some hair is visible, can be found on Hatiya Island.
A trekker escorted by a security guard is found on Saint Martin's Island.

steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official maps are not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends you play these maps instead:

  • A Balanced Bangladesh (map link) - 50k+ computer generated locations balanced with state streaking in mind.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise Bangladesh:

  • Plonk It Bangladesh (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It Bangladesh guide from step 2 to 3.

lm.name: Bangladesh
lm.note:
Bangladeshi licence plates are either white, black or turquoise.

NOTE: The turquoise plate can only be found in Bangladesh.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - All-White Wood Frame House Style
lm.note: Wood frame houses composed of exclusively solid-white, non-metallic panels are concentrated mainly in the area between Narayanganj and the Padma River.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Alternating Brick Corners
lm.note: This alternating brick pattern on the corners of buildings is seen in Rajshahi Division and Rangpur Division more commonly than in other parts of the country.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Barishal Architecture
lm.note: Some two-storey houses in or near Barishal Division have this characteristic tiered shape, featuring two separate roof levels with a narrower top floor and a wider bottom floor.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Barishal Market Houses
lm.note: Shophouses in Barishal Division are often characterised by a two-storey structure with a roof extending over a storefront on the bottom. The wall of the upper storey often has a wood frame and if there are windows, they may have metal shutters or blinds.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Chittagong Style Wood Frame Houses
lm.note: Wood frame houses in north-western Chittagong Division vary dramatically and display design elements not commonly found in other divisions. These include: (1) painted metal panels with diagonally-oriented corrugation (2) wood frames with rounded edges, and (3) friezes with floral designs under the eaves with a ‘carved’ look Note that the friezes should not be confused with the floral wallpaper friezes that can be found throughout the country.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Clay Houses
lm.note: Houses made of clay or mud appear in many parts of Bangladesh, but are most heavily concentrated within Rajshahi Division and along the western border with India.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Clay Houses with Decorative Scoring
lm.note: Many of the clay houses in the area south of Bogura are scored with decorative lines, often in arch, scallop, or grid shapes.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Diamond Pattern Shutters
lm.note: Closed metal shutters with patterns on them, usually coloured, are mostly found in the north-west of the country. Several patterns exist, but this diamond pattern is one of the most common and most reliable. Note that the same pattern is also quite common on metal doors in Gazipur District.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Dry Palm Fences
lm.note: Strings of dried or drying palm fronds, which can serve as a fence or screen, are a common sight in much of Barisal Division and Khulna Division. However, they can occasionally be found in all parts of Bangladesh.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Haor Basin Architecture
lm.note:
Around the western Haor Basin area, many of the small triangular gables have solid gable decorations. This is in contrast to the intricate lace-like gable decorations which are commonly seen elsewhere. The gable decorations in this area also sometimes have a distinctive ‘wavy’ shape.

Close to Mithamain, you may also see buildings featuring thick cornices and decorative arches in a distinctive style.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Harpoon Ridge Ends
lm.note: Harpoon-shaped ridge ends, ending in a long point and notched along the bottom, are found along the Khulna-Dhaka border. They are most concentrated just south of Magura.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Horizontal Corrugation Metal Houses
lm.note: Houses with metal sheet walls, with a horizontally-corrugated top sheet are by far most common in western Mymensingh Division.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Khulna Granaries
lm.note: In western Khulna Division, you can find small circular granaries with conical metal roofs. The walls can be made of various materials, including brick, metal, or woven materials.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Living Stick Fences
lm.note: ‘Living fences’ made partly from slender saplings (that sometimes look more like sticks) appear very frequently in the southern parts of Khulna Division and Barishal Division. They are found more rarely in other parts of Bangladesh.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Makeshift Balconies
lm.note: Slightly makeshift balconies made out of wood, scrap metal or plastic (as opposed to brick or concrete) can sometimes be seen attached to facades of buildings in Barishal Division.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Metal-Bamboo Fences
lm.note: Fences made from corrugated metal sheets with horizontal bamboo stick supports can be found in all divisions of Bangladesh, but are particularly common in Rangpur Division and Chittagong Division.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Metal-Bamboo Grid Houses
lm.note: Houses with metal sheet walls, reinforced with both horizontal and vertical bamboo on the outside, are commonly found in central Rangpur Division, as well as in the far west of Rajshahi Division. In Rangpur Division, the vertical bamboo sticks are usually noticeably thicker than the horizontal ones.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Metal-Woven Houses
lm.note: Houses with walls made out of a corrugated metal sheet at the bottom and woven bamboo at the top can be found in Rangpur Division and Chittagong Division.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Narrow Top Row Wood Frames
lm.note: In Mymensingh Division you will not see entire walls with exterior wood framing, but it is still somewhat common to see a narrow row or two of wooden frames along the top edge of walls. This design can also be found in Dhaka Division and north-western Chittagong Division.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Ornate Hanging Roof Trim
lm.note: You can find this type of decorative trim hanging from the eaves of roofs in a fairly large region of Bangladesh, primarily across Mymensingh, Dhaka, and Barishal divisions.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Outward-Facing Birdhead Ridge Ends
lm.note: Bird-shaped ridge ends can be found within Dhaka Division, south of Faridpur. There are a few different styles, but they always include distinct facial features such as a beak or eyes, and not just wings and a point for the head. To be a reliable clue, the bird’s head should be facing outward, away from the house; inward-facing counterparts appear sporadically in other regions.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Painted Woven Walls and Fences
lm.note: If you see structures made from painted woven bamboo, you should be in Chittagong Division.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Pigeon Pots
lm.note: In the far west of Rajshahi Division, you can sometimes find rows of clay pots hanging from the eaves of houses for pigeons to nest in.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Pointed Ridge Ends with Discs
lm.note: Ridge ends with a long point with one or more disc-shaped adornments feature prominently in Dhaka division, predominantly in the region south of the Padma River. There is some spillover into bordering parts of Khulna Division and Barisha Division. A second significant pocket of these ridge ends is found in the south-east of Rajshahi Division.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Raised Gables
lm.note: Houses with raised, stone roof edges, higher than the sheets or tiles of the roof, are most common in western Rajshahi Division but can also be found in Khulna Division.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Roof Shelves
lm.note: Houses with protruding concrete ledges, right above the window line and around most of the building, are common in central-western Bangladesh. Items, such as pots and dried crops, can sometimes be seen stored on top of them.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - String Net Fences
lm.note:
Fences made from white string netting appear with some regularity across south Bangladesh, particularly toward the southern tip of Barishal Division.

Be careful not to confuse these with wire fences and other types of net fencing such as the common blue mesh net fencing seen throughout the country.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Sylhet Charity Boxes
lm.note: Around the city of Sylhet you can commonly find these small, stone house-shaped boxes which serve primarily as donation boxes for local mosques.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Sylhet Walls
lm.note: Around Sylhet it is very common to find smooth concrete walls with vertical ribs. Even more unique to Sylhet are walls made of bricks with text on them.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Taco-Shaped Wing Ends
lm.note: ‘Taco’-shaped ridge ends with rounded, symmetrical wings often feature on roofs on both sides of the Padma River, just west of its confluence with the Brahmaputra River.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Tall Clay Houses
lm.note: Tall, multistorey clay houses are nearly exclusive to this large portion of Rajshahi Division.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Tall Triangular Roof Decorations
lm.note: Houses with these tall, ornate gable decorations over the top of the small triangular gables appear in two distinct clusters in the north and south of Dhaka Division.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Tarp Roofs and Fences
lm.note: While not exclusive to this area, Cox’s Bazar District features a high frequency of roofs carefully covered with tarp due to the extreme weather there. In this region, tarps will characteristically be held in place with a wooden or bamboo lattice. Tarp fences using the same style also appear in this area.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Tiled Roofs
lm.note: Roofs covered with clay tiles can often be seen in western Khulna Division, but also in some areas of Rajshahi Division.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Tobacco Curing Barns
lm.note: These **straw and clay structures with vents and metal flues **are used for curing tobacco leaves and are commonly found in the tobacco growing areas of northern Khulna Division. Tobacco leaves can often be seen hanging on racks nearby.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Turquoise Roofs
lm.note: Turquoise or teal-coloured metal roofs can be found nationwide, but are most common in Chittagong Division, particularly across Cox’s Bazar District. Neighbourhoods featuring multiple roofs in this colour are especially good clues for the region.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Twisted Loop Ridge Ends
lm.note: Twisted loop decorations about a pointed ridge end sometimes feature on roofs south of the Padma River in Dhaka Division. When viewed up close, they usually appear to be formed from two thin ‘wings’ twisted backward and touching at the points.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Wing Ridge Ends
lm.note: Wing-shaped ridge ends, often loosely resembling a bird or butterfly, are widespread in Bangladesh but are notably absent in the north-east and south-east of the country.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Wood Frame Houses
lm.note:
Walls covered with exterior wooden frames, usually in a grid (or staggered grid) pattern, can be found commonly in southern Dhaka Division, Barishal Division, and north-western Chittagong Division.

Various styles of these wood frame houses, explained in other locations for this map and at https://rmrg.me/guides/bangladesh/, can further narrow down your guess.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Wooden Frame Gable Covers
lm.note: Triangular frames bordering the small triangular gable can be found in central and central-northern Bangladesh, as well as in a small area in western Rajshahi District.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - Woven Jute Fences
lm.note: Fences made from loosely woven bundles of jute are mostly found south of the Padma River, especially in Dhaka Division. The tops can be left uneven or neatly trimmed. Occasionally other structures, such as sheds, feature walls with the same construction.

lm.name: ARCHITECTURE - X-Shaped Frame Rows
lm.note: To the west of the city of Dhaka, south of Savar, you may find houses with a row of X-shaped frames along the top of the outer wall.

lm.name: CULTURE - Buddhism
lm.note: Although there are Buddhist minority groups in every division of Bangladesh, the largest group by far resides in Chittagong Division. Useful clues to recognise these areas include Buddhist temples and stupas, iconography such as dharma wheels, statues of Buddha and Buddhist flags.

lm.name: CULTURE - Chakma
lm.note: The Chakma script, used by the Chakma Buddhist minority, can rarely be found in the northern half of the hilly interior of Chittagong.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Angular Fender Bars Roofed Cycle Rickshaw
lm.note: Roofed cycle rickshaws with angular fenders with painted metal bars on top can be found in Mymensingh Division. The roof will often be folded back.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Barishal Roofed Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Roofed cycle rickshaws with these distinctive rear axle ornaments are only found in Barishal Division. There are two common variants: a simpler design with an upside-down heart shape in the centre and a more ornate one with a circular design in the centre.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Bent Bar Rickshaws
lm.note: A high proportion of auto rickshaws in Mymensingh Division have a metal bar over the top of the front roof area with a slight but noticeable upward bend. They may or may not have small metal ball shapes on them, either on each side or along the bar. You see similar metal bars in other regions occasionally, but they are normally unbent.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Boomerang-Prow Boats
lm.note: Boats with an extended prow can be seen on the coast or on rivers near the coast in Barishal Division and Chittagong Division. Because they are not seen far inland, this can help confirm your proximity to the coast when you see them in river settings.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Brick Road Lining
lm.note: Roads lined by rows of small bricks (either raised or embedded into the ground) are most often found in the south-west, and less frequently in the north-west of the country.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Chariotlike Rickshaws
lm.note: Chariot-like cycle and auto rickshaws with this distinctive style of large passenger seat are only found between Gazipur and Mawna in Dhaka Division.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Chittagong Auto Rickshaws
lm.note: Auto rickshaws in Chittagong often feature a variety of decorations and characteristics which are unlikely to appear in other parts of Bangladesh. These include: (1) Long lines of Arabic calligraphy written above the windshield (not just the single word Allah, الله, which is commonplace) (2) Semicircular grill ornaments (as opposed to pointed or ‘onion-dome’-shaped) (3) Grill ornaments flanked by a pair of upward-pointing ‘bulbous cage’ metal ornaments. Most auto rickshaws in Chittagong do not have all of these features, but seeing one or more of them on an auto rickshaw is a good clue for this division.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Chittagong Roofed Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Roofed cycle rickshaws with multiple lines above the rear axle can be found in some areas of southern Chittagong Division and are particularly common in the city of Chittagong.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Colored Front Auto Rickshaws
lm.note: Green auto rickshaws in this part of western Chittagong Division will usually have all or half of the front painted in a different bright solid colour, such as yellow, red or blue. When half is painted it may be the upper or lower half. While it is possible to rarely find such auto rickshaws elsewhere, they will only constitute a majority in this area.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Cross Bench Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with a cross bench (oriented perpendicular to the driving direction) and often painted in a striped blue-red-yellow pattern can be found between Tangail and Dhaka.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Curly Dome Rickshaw Ornaments
lm.note: This distinctive grill ornament featuring two curled scroll shapes appears in Chittagong Division to the north of Chittagong . It remains a fairly-reliable indicator for this region even when positioned elsewhere on the rickshaw, such as on the side above the back wheels.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Double Rounded Cross Pattern Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Flatbed cycle rickshaws with this pattern of quarter circles and semicircles, forming a ‘double rounded cross’ pattern, can be seen in eastern Dhaka Division and across the border in Khulna Division, near Magura.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Jeeps
lm.note: These jeep-style utility vehicles appear predominantly in Chittagong division, especially in the Chittagong Hill Tracts.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Lime Piles
lm.note: Due to import regulations, at every major border crossing with India, there are long stretches of road surrounded by piles of lime. These are sometimes in the form of rocks and sometimes in the form of ground powder.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Long Bench Back Bars Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with long benches (oriented parallel to the driving direction) and decorative metal bars at the back can be found north-west of Naogaon. These rickshaws will not have a cross bench behind the driver's seat.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Long Bench Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with long benches (oriented parallel to the driving direction) and without rear decorations or a cross bench can be commonly seen in northern Rajshahi Division and south-eastern Rangpur Division.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Long Plank Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Flatbed cycle rickshaws with long planks, oriented parallel to the driving direction, can rarely be found all around the country, however they are by far most common in north-western Rangpur Division and rarely in north-western Mymensingh Division, along the border with India.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Metal Carts and Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Pulled carts and cycle rickshaws with metal cage-like frames are commonly used in Sylhet Division and rarely in Chittagong Division.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Metal Handle Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Flatbed cycle rickshaws with metal handles above the rear wheels can often be seen around the city of Khulna, in south-western Dhaka Division, and less commonly in Barishal Division. A variant with longer handles also exists in this area.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Moon Boats
lm.note: Strikingly-shaped moon boats are an iconic cultural emblem of Cox’s Bazar. You can sometimes spot them in actual use but you may also see them on public display.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Patgram Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Rickshaws similar to the U-bench cycle rickshaw, with two long benches and a cross bench in a ‘U’ formation, but with wooden vertical extensions visible on both sides of rear wheels, are only found around the town of Patgram in northern Rangpur Division.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Perpendicular Grids
lm.note: In much of southern Barishal Division and adjacent parts of Chittagong Division, and especially on Bhola Island and Hatiya Island, there are various areas which have N-S oriented grids.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Rectangular Frame Rickshaws
lm.note: Additionally, flatbed cycle rickshaws with a rectangular metal frame under the driver’s seat, are commonly found in far north-west Rangpur Division.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Rounded Cross Pattern Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Flatbed cycle rickshaws with this pattern of corner quarter circles, forming a ‘rounded cross’ pattern can often be seen in northern Khulna Division, east of Pabna in Rajshahi Division and in central Rajshahi Division.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Sadarpur Roofed Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with long benches and square roofs supported by colourful pillars can be found around the town of Sadarpur in south-western Dhaka Division. A variant with the roof extending over the driver’s seat also exists in this area.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - SMI Roofed Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: These cycle rickshaws with long benches and ridged roofs are only used on St. Martin’s Island, in the far south of Bangladesh.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - South Barishal Auto Rickshaws
lm.note: This grill ornament featuring a semicircle over an onion-dome shape appears on the front of electric auto rickshaws to the south of the city of Barishal, roughly between the Payra and Tetulia rivers.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Tunnel-like Roofed Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with arched tunnel-like roofs extending over the driver’s seat are only used in two separate areas near the border with India: south of Satkhira and south of Meherpur.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - U Bench Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with two long benches and a cross bench in a ‘U’ formation are commonly found in eastern Rajshahi Division and part of southern Rangpur Division.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - VIP Rickshaw Covers
lm.note: This distinctive style of roof covering is seen on some electric auto rickshaws in western Rajshahi Division and southern Rangpur Division. The covering usually features the text ‘VIP’ although custom variants with other initials also exist. The colour scheme can vary but will be two-tone or three-tone.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Welcome Rickshaws
lm.note: South and east of the city of Sylhet, you can somewhat commonly see auto rickshaws with the text ‘Well Come’ or ‘Welcome’ on the side roof area, above or behind the door.

lm.name: INFRASTRUCTURE - Wooden Fender Extension Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Flatbed cycle rickshaws with horizontal wooden extensions above the rear wheels are most commonly found north-east of Tangail and in part of southern Mymensingh Division, but can also be seen in Magura.

lm.name: LANDSCAPE - Chalan Beel
lm.note: The Chalan Beel is the largest low-lying basin after the Haor Basin. While you won’t find large flooded areas here, you’ll generally have a much more expansive landscape than typical for the country, with few trees. In this area you will also commonly find artificial ponds and haystacks by the roadside.

lm.name: LANDSCAPE - Cumilla Hills
lm.note: Apart from the Chittagong Hill Tracts and the Sylhet tea hills, Bangladesh is almost completely flat. The main other exception is a small N-S hill range just west of Cumilla, which can be distinguished from other hilly areas by the prevalence of Palmyra palms.

lm.name: LANDSCAPE - Dhaka Planned Towns
lm.note: Around Dhaka, you can find areas designated for future large-scale urban development, recognisable by the open, non-agricultural landscape and roads arranged in a grid-like pattern. Fenced-off plots without any buildings and high-rise buildings under construction can also be seen in these areas.

lm.name: LANDSCAPE - Haor Basin
lm.note: Large floodplains known as ‘haors’ make up much of the landscape of north-eastern Bangladesh. This area is known as the Haor Basin. In the dry season the floodplains resemble vast fields of rice or grasslands, often with almost nothing else in sight, while in the rainy season they get largely filled with water, giving the impression of large lakes.

lm.name: LANDSCAPE - Mirasharai Economic Zone
lm.note: The Mirasharai Economic Zone, located on the coast south of Feni, can be recognised by vast stretches of unused open land with industrial buildings in the distance. Roads in this area will often be lined with beach she-oaks and utility poles covered in ads.

lm.name: LANDSCAPE - Sal Tree Forest
lm.note: The Bengal plain has very few natural forests left, with most being found just north of Dhaka and in the far north of Dhaka Division. There is also a smaller forest near Dinajpur. These forests are composed of Sal trees (Shorea robusta).

lm.name: LANDSCAPE - Salt Ponds
lm.note: Salt evaporation ponds can be found near Pekua in Cox’s Bazar District.

lm.name: LANDSCAPE - Sundarbans
lm.note: The Sundarbans, located in the south-west corner of the country, are the largest mangrove forest in the world. The area has extensive boat coverage. Mangroves with their recognisable roots are always visible on the shore.

lm.name: LANDSCAPE - Water Plots
lm.note: In the far south of Khulna Division, you will find a much more open landscape than most of Bangladesh, with roads typically running through artificial water plots of varying sizes.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Banyan Trees
lm.note: Banyan trees (Ficus benghalensis) can be found in all parts of Bangladesh. However, examples featuring sprawling branches and abundant visible aerial roots appear more commonly in western Bangladesh, especially Rajshahi and Rangpur divisions, and are rarer in the east.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Date Palms
lm.note: Date palms (Phoenix sylvestris) with this jagged trunk shape appear toward the south and west of Bangladesh, and are especially common in Khulna Division nearer to the Indian border.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Disorganised Dried Dung Piles
lm.note: Dung being dried in messy piles often laid out on tarp or blankets is found in the central parts of the country.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Dragon Fruit
lm.note: Dragon fruit plantations can rarely be seen in various parts of Bangladesh, however they are by far most common west of Kaliganj in Khulna Division.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Dried Dung Sticks
lm.note: Dung ‘kebabs’ dried on sticks are commonly seen in two areas: in the south-west, especially Khulna Division, and in much of the central-north area of the country. They can also rarely be found in Barishal and northern Chittagong Division.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Eucalyptus Trees
lm.note: Eucalyptus trees appear across a wide area of Bangladesh. They are most associated with Rangpur Division, but are also prominent within the landscapes of several other regions of Bangladesh.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Giant Milkweed
lm.note: Giant milkweed (Calotropis gigantea) is a small shrub with thick oval leaves and pale flowers. It can mainly be found in the south-west of Bangladesh.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Giant Taro
lm.note: Giant taro (Alocasia macrorrhizos) is easily recognised by its large upward-pointing arrow-shaped leaves and can be seen most often in the south-west of the country.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Hay Houses
lm.note: Hay stacks that are ‘house-shaped’ with a ridge are found along the whole length of the western border with India. In the rest of the country, hay stacks are typically dome or bulb-shaped, ending at a single point.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Jute Bundles
lm.note: Neatly bound jute bundles with this hourglass-like shape are found in Rangpur Division.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Large Dried Dung Disks
lm.note: Dung ‘pizzas’ formed in the shape of large discs are often left to dry near settlements in the western Haor Basin.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Mango
lm.note: Mango plantations are overwhelmingly concentrated in the far west of Rajshahi Division. Even without their fruit, mango trees are recognisable by their dark green, spear-shaped leaves. The plantations typically consist of moderately spaced-out trees.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Mangrove Vegetation
lm.note: Mangrove vegetation, such as mangrove ferns (Acrostichum aureum) and less commonly mangrove palms (Nypa fruticans), can sometimes be seen growing in parts of Barishal and Khulna Division closest to the Sundarbans.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Marigold
lm.note: Marigold, easily recognisable by its vibrant orange and yellow flowers, while rare, is grown almost exclusively in Jashore and Jhenaidah districts in western Khulna Division.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Moringa
lm.note: Moringa (Moringa oleifera) is a small to medium-sized tree that is most recognisable by its delicate fractal-like (tripinnate) leaves consisting of small lentil-shaped leaflets. It is mainly found in the west of the country.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Neem
lm.note: Neem (Azadirachta indica) is a medium to large tree recognisable by its subdivided (pinnate) leaves with small triangular leaflets. It can be confused with other trees with pinnate leaves (such as for example African tulip tree), but these other trees won’t have the characteristic small triangular leaflets that neem has. Neem is commonly found along the western border and secondarily around the middle of the country.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Palmyra Palms
lm.note: Palmyra palms (Borassus flabellifer), while common throughout most of Bangladesh, are notably absent in the north-east and far north of the country.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Pineapple
lm.note: The majority of pineapple production in Bangladesh is found in Tangail District along the border with Mymensingh Division, in an area that is also characterised by slightly more orange soil than is typical for the country. Pineapple fields are easily recognisable by their rows of spiky leaf clusters. Pineapple plantations can also be found more rarely in the northern foothills of the Chittagong Hill Tracts.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Rubber
lm.note: Within Bangladesh, rubber tree plantations can mostly be found in the south of Sylhet Division and the areas of Chittagong Division shown on the map.

lm.name: VEGETATION - She-oaks
lm.note: Beach she-oaks (Casuarina equisetifolia) are most commonly encountered in lowland Chittagong Division.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Small Dried Dung Disks
lm.note: Smaller dung discs slapped onto walls or tree trunks to dry are generally more common in Rajshahi Division and southern Khulna Division, although are not a completely reliable indicator.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Tall Grass Clusters
lm.note: Roads lined with clumps of this tall, untufted grass are characteristic of Rajshahi and Rangpur divisions. They also appear occasionally in Mymensingh and northern Dhaka divisions. This particular grass species is known as ‘Vetiver’ (Chrysopogon zizanioides).

lm.name: VEGETATION - Tea
lm.note: Within Bangladesh, tea is grown in three distinct areas. Tea is by far most common in the hilly areas of Sylhet Division along the border with Tripura. It can also be found in the hills south of Tripura in Chittagong Division and in the far north-west in Rangpur Division. In Rangpur Division, the tea plants blend in with a more typical Bengali landscape.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Teak
lm.note: Within Bangladesh, teak (Tectona grandis) is grown mostly in the hilly parts of Chittagong and Sylhet Division, but can also be seen in the centre and west of the country. It can be recognised by its very large leaves and clustered flowers that are often visibly sticking out from the tree.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Tobacco
lm.note: Tobacco is mostly grown along the south bank of the Padma River, with most production coming from Kushtia District. Some tobacco fields can be found in the far north however, and also rarely in the hills of Chittagong. Tobacco has large, thick, slightly pale leaves with visible veins.

lm.name: VEGETATION - Turmeric
lm.note: While Bangladesh is one of the leading turmeric producers, you almost never see turmeric fields on street view. However roadside clusters of turmeric are a good indicator for the very far north, particularly Lalmonirhat District. Turmeric leaves are long and papery, and often curl inwards along the spine.

--- NOTE:

  • Make sure to check other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Bollard
lm.note:
Bangladesh uses red-and-white concrete bollards throughout the whole country.

NOTE: They can also be found in a square form instead of a circular form.

lm.name: Eastern Hills
lm.note: While most of Bangladesh is almost completely flat, in the eastern parts of Chittagong you may find fairly tall, forested and uncultivated hills.

lm.name: Canola
lm.note: Canola is a low-growing crop with yellow flowers that is used to make cooking oil. It is usually planted during the off-season for rice, making it extremely common north of Padma river in the state of Dhaka.

lm.name: Corn
lm.note:
Corn tends to be planted in the west of Bangladesh - large and medium-sized fields can be found in Rajshahi, Rangpur, western Mymensingh and northern Khulna.

Smaller patches of corn can be found in the south of Barishal, usually adjacent to other crops.

lm.name: early growth rice
lm.note:
Rice is the main agricultural crop in Bangladesh and is planted twice a year. The different rice seasons can be told apart by the height and colour of the rice and are very useful for regionguessing.

Short green rice that is barely sticking out of the water is known as early growth rice. Early growth rice can be seen in the states of Khulna, Mymensingh and south of Padma River in Dhaka.

  • rice meta only works in gen 4

lm.name: east-west ridge hazy
lm.note: A sizable east-west ridge can be seen on the Indian border from the northern parts of Sylhet and eastern Mymensingh. It is often obscured or diminished by heavy haze.

lm.name: fruit trees
lm.note: Standalone fruit trees in Bangladesh are most commonly seen in the states of Rajshahi and Rangpur. Fruit orchards with systematically planted trees, however, are concentrated near the Indian border in both states.

lm.name: Fully-grown rice
lm.note:
Fully-grown rice is characterised by being noticeably taller, as well as having a yellow or orange colour and fluffier tips - the fluffiness signifies that the rice is ripe. Fully-grown rice is mostly seen in the state of Rajshahi, but it is also present in Rangpur and Chittagong.

  • rice meta only works in gen 4

lm.name: Harvested rice
lm.note:
Harvested rice can be identified by its beige or brown colour and shorter, cut down appearance. It can be seen alongside fully-grown, unharvested rice as well as freshly planted early growth rice in adjacent fields. This is most commonly seen in the states of Sylhet and southern Khulna.

  • rice meta only works in gen 4

lm.name: hills
lm.note: While most of Bangladesh is almost completely flat, in the eastern parts of Chittagong you may find fairly tall, forested and uncultivated hills.

lm.name: hip roofs
lm.note:
Bangladesh has several distinct roof styles that create an east/west divide in the country.

The west, particularly the divisions of Rajshahi, Khulna and Dhaka, is dominated by hip roofs made of sheet metal. The states of Rangpur and Chittagong tend to have mixed roofs.

lm.name: Jute
lm.note: Jute is a tall-growing green crop which gets dried and used in the making of rugs, bags and other goods. Because of when the coverage was taken, jute can almost exclusively be found on Street View in Rangpur. In its dried state it can be found hanging off fences and drying on the roads anywhere in the country.

lm.name: rice middle of growing
lm.note:
Slightly taller rice, in the middle of growing, which still remains green, can be seen in the states of Rangpur, Barishal and Chittagong.

  • 22 Copyright is south-east
  • rice meta only works in gen 4

lm.name: Shitcam
lm.note: Shitcam coverage is only found in and around Dhaka.

lm.name: Sunflower fields
lm.note: Sunflower fields are found in the south of Barishal state.

lm.name: Tea
lm.note: Tea production in Bangladesh is concentrated in the highlands of southern Sylhet and, rarely, Chittagong.

lm.name: Tiled roofs
lm.note: Tiled roofs are uncommon in Bangladesh, but the ones you do see are of West Bengal origin, and are thus only found on the Indian border in the state of Khulna.

lm.name: triangular "window"
lm.note: In the east, you will commonly see sheet metal roofs with a triangular "window" just below the ridge of the roof. The state of Sylhet will exclusively have this style, which can also be seen in Chittagong, Mymensingh, eastern Rangpur and northern Dhaka.

lm.name: Vast rice fields
lm.note: Vast rice fields with almost nothing else in view can be seen in the border area between the states of Dhaka, Mymensingh and Sylhet.

lm.name: Watermelons
lm.note: Fields of watermelons can also be found in the south of Barishal.

lm.name: Bangaldesh - Metal Handle Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Flatbed cycle rickshaws with metal handles above the rear wheels can often be seen around the city of Khulna, in south-western Dhaka Division, and less commonly in Barishal Division. A variant with longer handles also exists in this area.

lm.name: Bangaldesh - Sadarpur Roofed Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with long benches and square roofs supported by colourful pillars can be found around the town of Sadarpur in south-western Dhaka Division. A variant with the roof extending over the driver’s seat also exists in this area.

lm.name: Angular Fender Bars Roofed Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Roofed cycle rickshaws with angular fenders with painted metal bars on top can be found in Mymensingh Division. The roof will often be folded back.

lm.name: Barishal Roofed Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Roofed cycle rickshaws with these distinctive rear axle ornaments are only found in Barishal Division. There are two common variants: a simpler design with an upside-down heart shape in the centre and a more ornate one with a circular design in the centre.

lm.name: Bent Bar Auto Rickshaws
lm.note: A high proportion of auto rickshaws in Mymensingh Division have a metal bar over the top of the front roof area with a slight but noticeable upward bend. They may or may not have small metal ball shapes on them, either on each side or along the bar. You see similar metal bars in other regions occasionally, but they are normally unbent.

lm.name: Chariotlike  Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Chariot-like cycle and auto rickshaws with this distinctive style of large passenger seat are only found between Gazipur and Mawna in Dhaka Division.

lm.name: Chittagong Auto Rickshaws
lm.note:
Auto rickshaws in Chittagong often feature a variety of decorations and characteristics which are unlikely to appear in other parts of Bangladesh. These include:

  • Long lines of Arabic calligraphy written above the windshield *(not just the single word Allah, الله, which is commonplace) *
  • Semicircular grill ornaments (as opposed to pointed or ‘onion-dome’-shaped)
  • Grill ornaments flanked by a pair of upward-pointing ‘bulbous cage’ metal ornaments Most auto rickshaws in Chittagong do not have all of these features, but seeing one or more of them on an auto rickshaw is a good clue for this division.

lm.name: Chittagong Roofed Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Roofed cycle rickshaws with multiple lines above the rear axle can be found in some areas of southern Chittagong Division and are particularly common in the city of Chittagong.

lm.name: Colored Front Auto Rickshaws
lm.note: Green auto rickshaws in this part of western Chittagong Division will usually have all or half of the front painted in a different bright solid colour, such as yellow, red or blue. When half is painted it may be the upper or lower half. While it is possible to rarely find such auto rickshaws elsewhere, they will only constitute a majority in this area.

lm.name: Cross Bench Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with a cross bench (oriented perpendicular to the driving direction) and often painted in a striped blue-red-yellow pattern can be found between Tangail and Dhaka.

lm.name: Curly Dome Auto Rickshaw Ornaments
lm.note: This distinctive grill ornament featuring two curled scroll shapes appears in Chittagong Division to the north of Chittagong . It remains a fairly-reliable indicator for this region even when positioned elsewhere on the rickshaw, such as on the side above the back wheels.

lm.name: Double Rounded Cross Pattern Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Flatbed cycle rickshaws with this pattern of quarter circles and semicircles, forming a ‘double rounded cross’ pattern, can be seen in eastern Dhaka Division and across the border in Khulna Division, near Magura.

lm.name: Jeeps
lm.note: These jeep-style utility vehicles appear predominantly in Chittagong division, especially in the Chittagong Hill Tracts.

lm.name: Long Bench Back Bars Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with long benches (oriented parallel to the driving direction) and decorative metal bars at the back can be found north-west of Naogaon. These rickshaws will not have a cross bench behind the driver's seat.

lm.name: Long Bench Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with long benches (oriented parallel to the driving direction) and without rear decorations or a cross bench can be commonly seen in northern Rajshahi Division and south-eastern Rangpur Division.

lm.name: Long Plank Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Flatbed cycle rickshaws with long planks, oriented parallel to the driving direction, can rarely be found all around the country, however they are by far most common in north-western Rangpur Division and rarely in north-western Mymensingh Division, along the border with India.

lm.name: Metal Carts and Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Pulled carts and cycle rickshaws with metal cage-like frames are commonly used in Sylhet Division and rarely in Chittagong Division.

lm.name: Patgram Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Similar cycle rickshaws with two long benches and a cross bench in a ‘U’ formation but with wooden vertical extensions visible on both sides of rear wheels, are only found around the town of Patgram in northern Rangpur Division.

lm.name: Rectangular Frame Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Additionally, flatbed cycle rickshaws with a rectangular metal frame under the driver’s seat, are commonly found in far north-west Rangpur Division.

lm.name: Rounded Cross Pattern Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Flatbed cycle rickshaws with this pattern of corner quarter circles, forming a ‘rounded cross’ pattern can often be seen in northern Khulna Division, east of Pabna in Rajshahi Division and in central Rajshahi Division.

lm.name: South Barishal Auto Rickshaws
lm.note: This grill ornament featuring a semicircle over an onion-dome shape appears on the front of electric auto rickshaws to the south of the city of Barishal, roughly between the Payra and Tetulia rivers.

lm.name: St. Martin’s Island Roofed Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: These cycle rickshaws with long benches and ridged roofs are only used on St. Martin’s Island, in the far south of Bangladesh.

lm.name: Tunnel-like Roofed Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with arched tunnel-like roofs extending over the driver’s seat are only used in two separate areas near the border with India: south of Satkhira and south of Meherpur.

lm.name: U Bench Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Cycle rickshaws with two long benches and a cross bench in a ‘U’ formation are commonly found in eastern Rajshahi Division and part of southern Rangpur Division.

lm.name: VIP Auto Rickshaw Covers
lm.note: This distinctive style of roof covering is seen on some electric auto rickshaws in western Rajshahi Division and southern Rangpur Division. The covering usually features the text ‘VIP’ although custom variants with other initials also exist. The colour scheme can vary but will be two-tone or three-tone.

lm.name: Welcome Auto Rickshaws
lm.note: South and east of the city of Sylhet, you can somewhat commonly see auto rickshaws with the text ‘Well Come’ or ‘Welcome’ on the side roof area, above or behind the door.

lm.name: Wooden Fender Cycle Rickshaws
lm.note: Flatbed cycle rickshaws with horizontal wooden extensions above the rear wheels are most commonly found north-east of Tangail and in part of southern Mymensingh Division, but can also be seen in Magura.

lm.name: Language
lm.note: The Bengali script features a continuous horizontal line at the top of each word. It resembles Devanagari (Hindi) but can be recognized by the many letters with triangular shapes. Bengali is an official language in Bangladesh and parts of eastern India(but coverage there is taken with "shit cam")

lm.name: "Indian" square roof tiles - "Indian" square roof tiles
lm.note: These square roof tiles (also common in West Bengal Indian) are found near the Western border with India, especially in Khulna division. Note: Contrary to the plonkit map used below, these can also be found in southern Rajshahi division and very rarely as far north as Rangpur division. They should still be clustered toward the Indian border in these divisions.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Barishal architecture - Barishal architecture
lm.note: Barishal division uses architectural styles that separate it from other parts of Bangladesh. One of the most recognizable designs is this two-story house featuring separate roofs for the first and second floors. The lower floor is wider than the upper floor on both sides, creating a distinct "shoulder" shape. Use of exterior timber framing for this house style is also common. Look out for slight variations on this style which can also be clues for Barishal division and its surrounding area. Credit: "The Bangladesh Doc" by Radu C, https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/u/1/d/e/2PACX-1vS6cGymuEpwoSaTI1BI7eteLSq5TlOo4Ky1GFFkN6lutRDua0nYJi95Yj-BZDKVTZxa38Ik96pf8cZH/pubhtml#gid=337612111

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Beach sheoaks - Beach sheoaks
lm.note: Beach sheoaks (Casuarina equisetifolia) are mostly found in coastal Chittagong, rarely in neighboring parts of Barishal division.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Bird - Bird-head ridge end
lm.note: In southwest Dhaka, to the west of Kasiana, you can sometimes find large, bird-shaped adornments at the ends of roof ridges. (Note that simpler "wing-shaped" roof ridge endings are common in across most of Bangladesh; however, large, detailed bird figures with a distinct head should steer you toward this location.)

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Buddhism - Buddhism
lm.note: Chittagong division has by far the largest Buddhist population, so any present-day Buddhist temples/sites (not ancient ruins) are a decent clue for Chittagong. Note that Islam remains the majority religion in Chittagong—Buddhist presence is just larger and much more noticeable here than in other divisions. Hinduism is fairly evenly distributed as a minority religion throughout Bangladesh. Be careful not to confuse Hindu and Buddhist temples. Learning to recognize characteristic architecture (e.g. use of stupas) and iconography (e.g. the 8-spoked dharma wheel) can be helpful for differentiating them.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Canola - Canola
lm.note: Yellow canola fields are usually found in Dhaka division.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Chittagong Timber frame houses - Chittagong Timber frame houses
lm.note: Timber-frame houses in northwestern Chittagong division (the area surrounding Cumilla) have a number of distinctive features which help differentiate them from timber-frame houses in Dhaka division and elsewhere, including use of painted corrugated metals, panels with diagonally oriented corrugation, floral designs, and articulated wood frame shapes. See doc for detailed descriptions of these features, and more info on Bangladesh timber frame house distribution: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Sezq-M_40qDTXgcXVo-OXnvA9mwBkL4mkiTPmWBTGP4/edit?tab=t.0

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Corn - Corn
lm.note: Larger cornfields are mostly found in the western divisions (Rangpur, Rajshahi, Khulna), more rarely in Myminsingh or Barishal. Tip: Look out for other evidence corn farming, such as piles of dried cornstalks which can be seen in towns even when cornfields are not visible.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Eucalyptus - Eucalyptus
lm.note: Eucalyptus is mostly found in the north, especially Rangpur and northern Rajshahi or Myminsingh divisions. However, they can be found less commonly throughout Dhaka and Chittagong divisions. In and around Rangpur, it is common to find eucalyptus trees growing in rows along roadsides.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Fruit orchards - Fruit orchards
lm.note: Orchards with neat rows of fruit trees such as mangoes are typically found in Rangpur and Rajshahi divisions, mostly near their northwest borders with India.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Harpoon - Harpoon-shaped ridge end
lm.note: The border area between Magura (Khulna divison) and Kasiana (Dhaka division) features some very localized roof ridge ending styles. These harpoon-shaped roof ridges are more common on the Khulna side. They appear as a long metal extension overhanging the end of the roof, and will be notched on the bottom. (This region features a lot of particularly long pointed roof edges in general, but they are not a reliable regionguessing clue unless there are notches on the bottom giving the "harpoon" shape).

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Hay - Hay
lm.note: House-shaped haystacks are mostly found in the western divisions of Rajshahi and Khulna. Storing haystacks on roof-tops is also a common practice in this region. Note that the more dome-shaped haystack style seen elsewhere in the country can also be found here.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Hilly terrain - Hilly terrain
lm.note: Hilly terrain can be found in parts of Sylhet and Chittagong divisions. The tallest, most impressive hills are found in the East and South of Chittagong division.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Hip roofs - Hip roofs
lm.note: Western “hip” roofs predominate in the South and West of the country.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Indian ridge - Indian ridge
lm.note: Mountain ridges to the north across the Indian border can rarely be seen along the northern edge of Sylhet. More rarely, similar ridges can be found in along the northern borders of Rangpur & Mymensingh.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Jute - Jute
lm.note: Jute is mostly found growing in Rangpur division (NW Bangladesh), and less often in Rajshahi. See this link for a map showing other regions where jute might be seen: https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Jute#/media/File:JuteCultivationArea.jpg

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Jute bundles - Jute bundles
lm.note: In addition to jute fields, upright jute bundles with this shape are another common sight in Rangpur.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Jute fences - Jute fences
lm.note: Although jute farming is most visible in Rangpur division, these loosely woven jute fences and walls can more often be found in Khulna and southern Dhaka divisions, especially along the border between the two.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Khulna granaries - Khulna granaries
lm.note: These small structures with a conical metal roof are a type of traditional granary typically found mostly in Khulna, especially in the West of that division.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Khulna mud houses - Khulna mud houses
lm.note: Mud structures in northern Khulna division often have this distinctive appearance, featuring a flat roof and pronounced horizontal ridges. Credit to Zetie from The Real Meta Research Group discord for identifying these as tobacco curing barns.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Large triangular roof decoration - Large triangular roof decoration
lm.note: These large, triangular decorations on window roofs are found mainly northeast of Tangail within Dhaka division. Often white, but can be colorful as well. (Note that if you see one of these attachments on a house with exterior timber frames, you are likely to be south of the city of Dhaka.)

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Moon boat - Moon boat
lm.note: These distinctively-shaped boats are a very recognizable part of the cultural heritage of Cox's Bazar. They are sometimes seen displayed along the southern coast of Chittagong division, or can be encountered in actual use (rare on streetview).

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Mud houses  - Mud houses - Decorative lines
lm.note: Mud houses with decorative scoring, typically in arch or "scallop" shapes, can be seen in a small region south of the city of Bogura (Rajshahi division). The scoring is sometimes fairly faint and can be difficult to spot from a distance.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Mud houses - Mud houses
lm.note: Mud houses can be found in the western divisions of Bangladesh. They are most densely concentrated in Rajshahi with significant numbers in northern Khulna and western Rangpur. Another pocket of mud houses can be found in south/central Chittagong, so check other clues such as roof type before guessing. Map credit: https://www.tslr.net/2007/07/mud-houses-of-bangladesh.html

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Pineapple - Pineapple
lm.note: A high density of pineapple fields in flat terrain can be found in NW Dhaka division and bordering areas of southern Myminsingh division. The area near Garobazar is especially dense with pineapple plantations, often growing alongside banana plantations (although bananas in general are more widespread found throughout the country). Note: Pineapple fields in hilly terrain are occasionally encountered in Sylhet and Chittagong divisions.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Pointed ridge end with rings - Pointed ridge end with rings
lm.note: Throughout Bangladesh you can find examples of roofs with a protruding "point" at the end of the top ridge. Pointed roof ridges featuring one or more disc-shaped "rings" are useful for regionguessing. These roofs most often appear in Dhaka division south of the Padma River. Occasionally you will also find these in Rajshahi division, with some minor spillover in bordering Khulna division.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Rangpur grass - Rangpur grass
lm.note: These tall green grass clusters are common to find lining roadsides in Rangpur division (NW Bangladesh). They may more rarely be found in other northern divisions of Bangladesh.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Rubber trees - Rubber trees
lm.note: Rubber tree plantations are mostly found in hilly areas in the east, within Sylhet and Chittagong divisions. An easy way to recognize them is that they often (though not always) feature diagonal cuts along the trunks, resulting from the process of harvesting latex.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Sal forests - Sal forests
lm.note: These relatively uniform forests dominated by sal trees (Shorea robusta) are common in the north central and northwest parts of Dhaka division. They should be found on flatter terrain. See the map/link below for a more precise distribution of sal forests in Bangladesh. Hillier terrain might help to differentiate Dhaka sal forests from those found in Sylhet. Credit: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Map-showing-the-distribution-of-moist-deciduous-Sal-Shorea-robusta-forests-of_fig1_210196050

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Southern tree stands - Southern tree stands
lm.note: In the southern divisions of Bangladesh, you can often find this type of humid, dense, tightly-packed tree stands or forests. They often feature areca palms mixed with other narrow-trunked trees. This is particularly characteristic of Barishal, but can also be found in Khulna and Chittagong divisions. Note that you can still find plenty of other habitats, includnig wide-open crop fields, in each of these regions.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Sunflowers - Sunflowers
lm.note: Sunflower fields are concentrated in southern Barishal division.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Sylhet brick - Sylhet brick
lm.note: Sylhet division brick walls (NE of Bangladesh) often feature these distinctive bricks with letters on them. In general cement and brick walls are common in Sylhet division where fences might be used in other parts of Bangladesh.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Tarp roofs - Tarp roofs
lm.note: Due to extreme weather, roofs carefully covered with tarp are a common sight in the Cox’s Bazar district in southern Chittagong division. (This is not 100% exclusive to Chittagong, so consider other clues).

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Tea - Tea
lm.note: Tea plantations are very common in southern Sylhet division, also fairly common in the rest of Sylhet and the part of Chittagong near the southern border of Tripura India. In these divisions, tea typically grows in sprawling plantations on hilly terrain, often raised above the road.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Tea, Rangpur - Tea, Rangpur
lm.note: While tea is mostly found in the east of Bangladesh, tea can more rarely be encountered in northern Rangpur. Whereas the stereotypical tea plantation in Sylhet or Chittagong is sprawling and may or may not be hilly, tea plantations in Rangpur should be quite flat and may appear smaller in area. They should not be raised up above the height of the road. Credit: Atomo from "The Real Meta Research Group" Discord

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Teal roofs - Teal roofs
lm.note: The southernmost part of Chittagong division, roughly centered around Cox's Bazar, makes heavy use of these teal or turquoise metal roofs. Credit: Atomo from "The Real Meta Research Group" Discord

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Timber frame houses - Timber frame houses
lm.note: Timber frame houses are found in the South of Dhaka division, and to a lesser extent in Barishal division and bordering areas of Chittagong. In Dhaka division, they are often white, but they can also be painted in other solid colors or feature plain corrugated metal panels. Bonus: In many parts of Dhaka division you will see a mix of solid white panels and other types, but if you see only solid white panels all the way around the building, you are almost certainly in the area directly south of Dhaka city, along the Padma river. See doc for more on Bangladesh timber frame house distribution: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Sezq-M_40qDTXgcXVo-OXnvA9mwBkL4mkiTPmWBTGP4/edit?tab=t.0

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Tobacco - Tobacco
lm.note: Tobacco is mostly grown in northern Khulna division, especially around the city of Kushtia.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Vast rice fields - Vast rice fields
lm.note: An extremely vast landscape dominated by rice fields stretching to the horizon in found around the northeast corner of Dhaka division, and neighboring parts of Myminsingh and Sylhet, roughly centered around Mithamain.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Watermelons - Watermelons
lm.note: Watermelon fields are concentrated in southern Barishal division.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: West Rajshahi pigeon pots - West Rajshahi pigeon pots
lm.note: Rows of pots hanging from the eaves of roofs are seen in the far west of Rajshahi division (NW of Rajshahi city). They mostly feature on two-story mud/clay houses. The pots are intended for pigeons to nest in.

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Western roofs - Western roofs
lm.note: In the western divisions of Rangpur, Rajshahi, and Khulna, this style of roof can be found, where the short end of the exterior wall extends in a triangle shape above the rooftop. (Note these roofs can rarely be found in other parts of Bangladesh, so check for other clues before guessing. Another notable cluster of similar roofs can be found along the eastern border with Tripura, India).

lm.map: A Learnable Bangladesh - real-world metas only
lm.name: Window roofs - Window roofs
lm.note: Eastern “window” roofs predominate in the North and East of the country. Note: In contrast to the plonkit guide map used below, this roof type was encountered routinely in Barishal division during creation of this map. It was still in the minority there, but it is not uncommon. However, it was practically never found in Khulna or Rajshahi divisions.

lm.note: Timber framed top rows with a line of “X” panels across the top can be found west of Dhaka (city), just south of Savar. See doc for more on Bangladesh timber frame house distribution: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Sezq-M_40qDTXgcXVo-OXnvA9mwBkL4mkiTPmWBTGP4/edit?tab=t.0

lm.name: Moulvibazar - Moulvibazar
lm.note:
মৌলভীবাজার

মৌ = ম (ma) + ৌ (ou) = মৌ (mou)

ল = la (inherent o)

ভী = ভ (bha) + ী (ī) = ভী (bhī)

বা = ব (ba) + া (ā) = বা (bā)

জা = জ (ja) + া (ā) = জা (jā)

র = ra (inherent o)

lm.name: Munshiganj - Munshiganj
lm.note:
মুন্সীগঞ্জ

মু = ম (ma) + ু (u) = মু (mu)

ন্সী = ন (na) + ্ (hasanta) + স (sha/sa) = ন্স (ns) + ী (ī) = ন্সী (nsī)

গঞ্জ = গ (ga) + ঞ্জ [ঞ (ña) + ্ (hasanta) + জ (ja) = ঞ্জ (nj)] = গঞ্জ (gonj)

Latin: Munshiganj (MSJ)

lm.name: Mymensingh - Mymensingh
lm.note:
ময়মনসিংহ

ম = ma (inherent o)

য় = ya (antastha ya, semivowel)

ম = ma (inherent o)

ন = na (inherent o)

সিং = স (sha/sa) + ি (i) = সি (si) + ং (anusvara, nasal 'ng') = সিং (sing)

হ = ha (inherent o)

Latin: Mymensingh (MYM)

lm.name: Naogaon - Naogaon
lm.note:
নওগাঁ

ন = na (inherent o)

ও = independent vowel o

গাঁ = গ (ga) + া (ā) + ঁ (chandrabindu, nasalization) = গাঁ (gān)

Note: ঁ (chandrabindu) nasalizes the vowel — here ā becomes ān.

Latin: Naogaon (NGN)

lm.name: Narail - Narail
lm.note:
নড়াইল

ন = na (inherent o)

ড়া = ড় (ṛa) + া (ā) = ড়া (ṛā)

ই = independent vowel i

ল = la (inherent o)

Note: ড় is the retroflex flap — unique to Bengali, it sounds like a soft 'r' or 'ṛ'.

Latin: Narail (NRL)

lm.name: Narayanganj - Narayanganj
lm.note:
নারায়ণগঞ্জ

না = ন (na) + া (ā) = না (nā)

রা = র (ra) + া (ā) = রা (rā)

য় = ya (antastha ya)

ণ = ṇa (cerebral nasal, inherent o)

গঞ্জ = গ (ga) + ঞ্জ [ঞ (ña) + ্ (hasanta) + জ (ja) = ঞ্জ (nj)] = গঞ্জ (gonj)

Latin: Narayanganj (NRJ)

lm.name: Narsingdi - Narsingdi
lm.note:
নরসিংদী

ন = na (inherent o)

র = ra (inherent o)

সিং = স (sha/sa) + ি (i) = সি (si) + ং (anusvara) = সিং (sing)

দী = দ (da) + ী (ī) = দী (dī)

Latin: Narsingdi (NSD)

lm.name: Natore - Natore
lm.note:
নাটোর

না = ন (na) + া (ā) = না (nā)

টো = ট (ṭa) + ো (o) = টো (ṭo)

র = ra (inherent o)

Note: ট is a retroflex stop — tongue tip curls back to touch the palate.

Latin: Natore (NTR)

lm.name: Netrokona - Netrokona
lm.note:
নেত্রকোনা

নে = ন (na) + ে (e) = নে (ne)

ত্র = ত (ta) + ্ (hasanta) + র (ra) = ত্র (tra)

কো = ক (ka) + ো (o) = কো (ko)

না = ন (na) + া (ā) = না (nā)

Note: নেত্র (netra) means 'eye' in Sanskrit/Bengali.

Latin: Netrokona (NTK)

lm.name: Nilphamari - Nilphamari
lm.note:
নীলফামারী

নী = ন (na) + ী (ī) = নী (nī)

ল = la (inherent o)

ফা = ফ (pha) + া (ā) = ফা (phā)

মা = ম (ma) + া (ā) = মা (mā)

রী = র (ra) + ী (ī) = রী (rī)

Latin: Nilphamari (NLF)

lm.name: Noakhali - Noakhali
lm.note:
নোয়াখালী

নো = ন (na) + ো (o) = নো (no)

য়া = য় (ya) + া (ā) = য়া (yā)

খা = খ (kha) + া (ā) = খা (khā)

লী = ল (la) + ী (ī) = লী (lī)

Latin: Noakhali (NKH)

lm.name: Pabna - Pabna
lm.note:
পাবনা

পা = প (pa) + া (ā) = পা (pā)

ব = ba (inherent o)

না = ন (na) + া (ā) = না (nā)

Latin: Pabna (PBN)

lm.name: Panchagarh - Panchagarh
lm.note:
পঞ্চগড়

প = pa (inherent o)

ঞ্চ = ঞ (ña/nya) + ্ (hasanta) + চ (cha) = ঞ্চ (nch)

গ = ga (inherent o)

ড় = ṛa (retroflex flap, inherent o)

Note: পঞ্চ (pancha) means 'five' — the same root as 'penta-'.

Latin: Panchagarh (PCG)

lm.name: Patuakhali - Patuakhali
lm.note:
পটুয়াখালী

প = pa (inherent o)

টু = ট (ṭa) + ু (u) = টু (ṭu)

য়া = য় (ya) + া (ā) = য়া (yā)

খা = খ (kha) + া (ā) = খা (khā)

লী = ল (la) + ী (ī) = লী (lī)

Latin: Patuakhali (PTK)

lm.name: Pirojpur - Pirojpur
lm.note:
পিরোজপুর

পি = প (pa) + ি (i) = পি (pi)

রো = র (ra) + ো (o) = রো (ro)

জ = ja (inherent o)

পু = প (pa) + ু (u) = পু (pu)

র = ra (inherent o)

Latin: Pirojpur (PRJ)

lm.name: Rajbari - Rajbari
lm.note:
রাজবাড়ী

রা = র (ra) + া (ā) = রা (rā)

জ = ja (inherent o)

বা = ব (ba) + া (ā) = বা (bā)

ড়ী = ড় (ṛa) + ী (ī) = ড়ী (ṛī)

Note: রাজবাড়ী literally means 'king's house' — রাজ (king) + বাড়ী (house).

Latin: Rajbari (RJB)

lm.name: Rajshahi - Rajshahi
lm.note:
রাজশাহী

রা = র (ra) + া (ā) = রা (rā)

জ = ja (inherent o)

শা = শ (sha) + া (ā) = শা (shā)

হী = হ (ha) + ী (ī) = হী (hī)

Latin: Rajshahi (RJS)

lm.name: Rangamati - Rangamati
lm.note:
রাঙামাটি

রা = র (ra) + া (ā) = রা (rā)

ঙা = ঙ (nga) + া (ā) = ঙা (ngā)

মা = ম (ma) + া (ā) = মা (mā)

টি = ট (ṭa) + ি (i) = টি (ṭi)

Note: ঙ is the velar nasal — the 'ng' sound as in 'sing'.

Latin: Rangamati (RGM)

lm.name: Rangpur - Rangpur
lm.note:
রংপুর

রং = র (ra) + ং (anusvara, nasal 'ng') = রং (rang)

পু = প (pa) + ু (u) = পু (pu)

র = ra (inherent o)

Note: ং (anusvara) is a pure nasal sound — always 'ng' as in 'sing', never 'n' or 'm'.

Latin: Rangpur (RGP)

lm.name: Satkhira - Satkhira
lm.note:
সাতক্ষীরা

সা = স (sha/sa) + া (ā) = সা (sā)

ত = ta (inherent o)

ক্ষী = ক (ka) + ্ (hasanta) + ষ (ṣha) = ক্ষ (kṣha/ksha) + ী (ī) = ক্ষী (kṣhī)

রা = র (ra) + া (ā) = রা (rā)

Note: ক্ষ is a conjunct of ক and ষ, pronounced 'ksha'.

Latin: Satkhira (STK)

lm.name: Shariatpur - Shariatpur
lm.note:
শরীয়তপুর

শ = sha (inherent o)

রী = র (ra) + ী (ī) = রী (rī)

য় = ya (antastha ya, semivowel)

ত = ta (inherent o)

পু = প (pa) + ু (u) = পু (pu)

র = ra (inherent o)

Latin: Shariatpur (SRP)

lm.name: Sherpur - Sherpur
lm.note:
শেরপুর

শে = শ (sha) + ে (e) = শে (she)

র = ra (inherent o)

পু = প (pa) + ু (u) = পু (pu)

র = ra (inherent o)

Latin: Sherpur (SHP)

lm.name: Sirajganj - Sirajganj
lm.note:
সিরাজগঞ্জ

সি = স (sha/sa) + ি (i) = সি (si)

রা = র (ra) + া (ā) = রা (rā)

জ = ja (inherent o)

গঞ্জ = গ (ga) + ঞ্জ [ঞ (ña) + ্ (hasanta) + জ (ja) = ঞ্জ (nj)] = গঞ্জ (gonj)

Note: গঞ্জ (gonj) means 'market town' — a very common suffix in Bangladesh district names.

Latin: Sirajganj (SRJ)

lm.name: Sunamganj - Sunamganj
lm.note:
সুনামগঞ্জ

সু = স (sha/sa) + ু (u) = সু (su)

না = ন (na) + া (ā) = না (nā)

ম = ma (inherent o, suppressed before following consonant)

গঞ্জ = গ (ga) + ঞ্জ [ঞ (ña) + ্ (hasanta) + জ (ja) = ঞ্জ (nj)] = গঞ্জ (gonj)

Latin: Sunamganj (SNJ)

lm.name: Sylhet - Sylhet
lm.note:
সিলেট

সি = স (sha/sa) + ি (i) = সি (si)

লে = ল (la) + ে (e) = লে (le)

ট = ṭa (retroflex stop, inherent o)

Note: In Bengali, স is pronounced 'sh' (like শ), so সিলেট sounds like 'Sillet'.

Latin: Sylhet (SYL)

lm.name: Tangail - Tangail
lm.note:
টাঙ্গাইল

টা = ট (ṭa) + া (ā) = টা (ṭā)

ঙ্গা = ঙ (nga) + ্ (hasanta) + গ (ga) = ঙ্গ (nga) + া (ā) = ঙ্গা (ngā)

ই = independent vowel i

ল = la (inherent o)

Note: ট is a retroflex stop — distinct from ত (dental t). Both exist in Bengali and look similar at first glance.

Latin: Tangail (TGL)

lm.name: Thakurgaon - Thakurgaon
lm.note:
ঠাকুরগাঁও

ঠা = ঠ (ṭha) + া (ā) = ঠা (ṭhā)

কু = ক (ka) + ু (u) = কু (ku)

র = ra (inherent o)

গাঁ = গ (ga) + া (ā) + ঁ (chandrabindu) = গাঁ (gān)

ও = independent vowel o

Note: ঠ is an aspirated retroflex stop — tongue curls back, with a puff of air.

Latin: Thakurgaon (TKG)

top.html:
Bangladeshi licence plates are either white, black or turquoise.

NOTE: The turquoise plate can only be found in Bangladesh.

top.html:
The Bengali script features a continuous horizontal line at the top of each word. It has a similar look to Devanagari (Hindi and Nepali), however it can usually be recognised by the many letters featuring triangular shapes.

NOTE: Bengali is an official language in Bangladesh and parts of eastern India.
top.raw: The Bengali script features a continuous **horizontal line** at the top of each word. It has a similar look to [Devanagari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devanagari) (Hindi and Nepali), however it can usually be recognised by the many letters featuring triangular shapes. NOTE: Bengali is an official language in Bangladesh and parts of eastern India.

In Generation 3 coverage, these three cars can be seen in Bangladesh: the red mirror with bars, classic white and striped white car.
